issues.detail: Error handling is limited to the parallel-run snippet and a few guideline notes, with no coverage of API rejections, rate limits (429), session timeouts, or CDP connection failures.
The Stagehand section gives no runnable code and defers to the README, and the persistent-context example omits the login step and the connect step.
Both examples are prose descriptions of what the agent does, with no concrete code, selectors, or sample output.

scenarios.name: proxy-scrape-blocked-retailer
scenarios.rationale: A satisfies nearly every rubric item (proxies: true, region, connectOverCDP, env API key, finally close, replay URL) but prints the replay URL before the try and not in the finally block; B omits the required region option entirely, though it otherwise covers the proxy, CDP, env key, finally close, and replay URL (printed again in finally).

scenarios.name: persistent-login-context-nightly
scenarios.rationale: Both create a context, log in with persist: true, and reuse it with persist: false. A explicitly gives both required warnings: wait a few seconds after closing the persist: true session, and don't run two sessions on one context at once. B covers release-before-reuse and concurrency too, but it never says to wait a few seconds. It also says several persist: false sessions can share a context, which partly contradicts the rubric's one-at-a-time warning. B's use of projectId in contexts.create is a slight deviation, and its added caveats don't earn rubric credit.

scenarios.name: parallel-titles-with-concurrency-limit
scenarios.rationale: Both use a worker pool (not fixed batches) and no Promise.allSettled, but B's tasks never throw and record errors, and its retry covers failures; B lacks a finally around sessions.create but closes the browser in finally, while A closes in finally plus releases the session; A records errors too, so they are close, with B slightly closer due to simpler direct structure and explicit acknowledgement of the deviation from batches.
